extracted.intended_audience: readers of political philosophy, students/scholars of democracy and religion, clergy and policymakers interested in religion's role in democratic societies
extracted.subtask_description: Expository guidance (from Tocqueville) about how religions, clergy, and democratic institutions should comport themselves and adapt in democratic societies; includes prescriptive principles and explanations of social causes and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religions should confine themselves within the circle of spiritual matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The circle within which they seek to bound the human intellect ought therefore to be carefully traced, and beyond its verge the mind should be left in entire freedom to its own guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religions risk not being believed at all if they seek to extend their power beyond religious matters; the gospel 'only speaks of the general relations of men to God and to each other--beyond which it inculcates and imposes no point of faith.' Religious authority should not unduly intrude into secular/political domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold fast to principal articles of faith but avoid binding secondary accessories
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal opinions which constitute belief... must be very carefully distinguished from the accessories connected with them. Religions are obliged to hold fast to the former... but they should take good care not to bind themselves in the same manner to the latter at a time when everything is in transition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish core doctrines (immutable) from ritual/formal practices (adaptable). In democratic ages, retain essential dogma while allowing flexibility in rites and external forms to avoid alienating the populace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the number and intrusiveness of external observances in democratic periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Religions ought to assume fewer external observances in democratic periods than at any others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Men in ages of equality are impatient of forms and predisposed to attach secondary importance to public-worship details; excessive ceremonial will reduce a religion to a band of fanatical zealots amid an infidel people. Keep ritual only to what is 'absolutely necessary to perpetuate the doctrine itself.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear, precise, intelligible, and lasting solutions to fundamental questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The first object and one of the principal advantages of religions, is to furnish to each of these fundamental questions a solution which is at once clear, precise, intelligible to the mass of mankind, and lasting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because most people lack leisure or capacity to resolve ultimate questions (God, soul, duty) by private reason, religion's utility in democratic ages is to offer accessible, stable answers that guide action and prevent moral confusion and social enervation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy should stand aloof from secular affairs and limit their jurisdiction to the spiritual
rubrics_metrics.description: In America religion is a distinct sphere, in which the priest is sovereign, but out of which he takes care never to go... Within its limits he is the master of the mind; beyond them, he leaves men to themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministers should avoid participation in party altercations and secular governance; by confining themselves they retain authority and avoid conflict with prevailing public opinion, thereby preserving religious influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy should respect and not needlessly oppose majority public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: All the American clergy know and respect the intellectual supremacy exercised by the majority; they never sustain any but necessary conflicts with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting general opinions of their country and age, clergy secure public support for religion and avoid antagonizing democratic sensibilities. Religion that sustains only necessary conflicts will be reinforced by public opinion rather than opposed to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion should regulate but not attempt to eradicate the natural love of well-being
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief concern of religions is to purify, to regulate, and to restrain the excessive and exclusive taste for well-being which men feel at periods of equality; but they would err in attempting to control it completely or to eradicate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting to eliminate material desires would provoke backlash; instead, religions should channel desire for prosperity into honest means and moderate excess rather than seek total renunciation of worldly goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: In democratic ages religions gain strength by aligning with prevailing ideas of unity and impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: When the conditions of society are becoming more equal... Men living in democratic ages are therefore very prone to shake off all religious authority; but, on the other hand, it imbues them with the taste and the idea of unity, simplicity, and impartiality in the power which governs society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religions that present single, uniform authority and general doctrines (unity, simplicity) may attract democratically minded populations; Catholic discipline and unity can appeal despite doctrinal surprises, if political antagonisms lessen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make disputed or theoretical subjects part of daily practical occupation to correct excessive generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: If there be a subject upon which a democratic people is peculiarly liable to abandon itself, blindly and extravagantly, to general ideas, the best corrective that can be used will be to make that subject a part of the daily practical occupation of that people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical engagement forces examination of particulars and exposes weaknesses in abstract theories. Democratic institutions that involve citizens in governance moderate blind attachment to general theory by compelling attention to details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect democratic minds to favor broad, general ideas due to limited leisure and desire for quick success
rubrics_metrics.description: Men who live in ages of equality have a great deal of curiosity and very little leisure... Such men are prone to general ideas because they spare them the trouble of studying particulars; they contain... a great deal in a little compass, and give, in a little time, a great return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this tendency as a social fact: policies, religious messaging, and education in democratic societies should account for the public's appetite for simplified, general doctrines and the risks of superficiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of pantheism's appeal under democratic conditions favoring unity and loss of individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: When the conditions of society are becoming more equal... the human mind seeks to embrace a multitude of different objects at once; the idea of unity so possesses itself of man... he seeks to expand and to simplify his conception by including God and the universe in one great whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantheistic systems, which 'destroy the individuality of man,' are especially seductive in democracies; defenders of individual human dignity and classical theism should 'struggle and combine' against such tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy encourages belief in indefinite human perfectibility, affecting social practices
rubrics_metrics.description: In proportion as castes disappear... the image of an ideal perfection, forever on the wing, presents itself to the human mind... he tends unceasingly towards that unmeasured greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This philosophical premise influences behavior (e.g., preference for shorter-lived but more progressive goods). Policymakers and cultural actors should anticipate and understand how belief in progress shapes institutions and practices.
